At the beginning of 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of a "smartphone monopoly."

Over the past two years, Apple has publicly opposed the case on multiple occasions. According to Bloomberg, the Department of Justice and Apple are now in settlement negotiations over the lawsuit.

Bloomberg noted that Apple has put forward "multiple proposals" this year in an attempt to reach a settlement with the Department of Justice:

The report also cautioned that although negotiations are still ongoing, there is no guarantee that Apple and the Department of Justice will ultimately reach an agreement.

The Department of Justice's antitrust lawsuit against Apple mainly revolves around five areas of the iPhone user experience: super apps, cloud streaming games, third-party messaging apps, third-party smartwatches, and third-party digital wallets.

Over the past year, Apple has made significant changes to address the issues of concern to the Department of Justice, including adding RCS support in the Messages app, launching a brand-new "Mini App Partner Program" on the App Store, and enhancing the openness of the iPhone NFC chip.

Whether these changes will satisfy the Department of Justice remains unknown. Admittedly, political factors are also involved, a point Bloomberg also mentioned:

Apple and the Department of Justice recently submitted a joint status report to the court to update the case's progress. In addition, Apple won a dispute earlier this week over the discovery of documents obtained from a federal government agency related to the Department of Justice's case.

9to5Mac's view

If Apple and the Department of Justice ultimately reach a settlement, it would significantly ease the burden on John Ternus, who is set to take over as Apple's CEO in September.
